chmmc-cmm-2023-team-01.title: Count common multiples
chmmc-cmm-2023-team-01.body:
Switches $A,B,C$ are on exactly at multiples of $20,21,22$, so $T=\operatorname{lcm}(20,21,22)=4620$.

Two switches are on together exactly at multiples of the lcm of their periods: $\operatorname{lcm}(20,21)=420$, $\operatorname{lcm}(21,22)=462$, $\operatorname{lcm}(20,22)=220$. A time $0<t<T$ cannot have all three on, so no time is counted twice.

The number of such times for each pair is $\frac{4620}{420}-1=10$, $\frac{4620}{462}-1=9$, $\frac{4620}{220}-1=20$. Total $10+9+20=39$.

**Answer: 39**

chmmc-cmm-2023-team-01.title: Check by listing
chmmc-cmm-2023-team-01.body:
A direct computer-style scan of $t=1,\dots,4619$ counting the $t$ divisible by at least two of $20,21,22$ gives the same count $39$.

**Answer: 39**

chmmc-cmm-2023-team-02.title: Count the three sets
chmmc-cmm-2023-team-02.body:
There are $9\cdot10=90$ three-digit palindromes $\overline{aba}$. The three-digit multiples of $11$ run from $110$ to $990$, so there are $\frac{990-110}{11}+1=81$.

$\overline{aba}$ is divisible by $11$ iff $a-b+a=2a-b\equiv0\pmod{11}$, i.e. $b=2a$ or $b=2a-11$ with $0\le b\le9$. This gives $(a,b)=(1,2),(2,4),(3,6),(4,8),(6,1),(7,3),(8,5),(9,7)$: $8$ numbers.

So $A=\frac8{90}$ and $B=\frac8{81}$, and
$$B-A=\frac{8}{81}-\frac{8}{90}=\frac{8\,(90-81)}{81\cdot90}=\frac{72}{7290}=\frac{4}{405}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{4}{405}$**

chmmc-cmm-2023-team-03.title: Find $r_k$ and telescope
chmmc-cmm-2023-team-03.body:
The arithmetic condition gives $a_{4k+1}=2a_{4k}-a_{4k-1}$ and $a_{4k+2}=3a_{4k}-2a_{4k-1}$. With $r_k=a_{4k}/a_{4k-1}$ we get
$$r_{k+1}=\frac{a_{4k+2}}{a_{4k+1}}=\frac{3a_{4k}-2a_{4k-1}}{2a_{4k}-a_{4k-1}}=\frac{3r_k-2}{2r_k-1}.$$
Since $r_1=4$, induction gives $r_k=\frac{6k-2}{6k-5}$: indeed if $r_k=\frac{6k-2}{6k-5}$ then $r_{k+1}=\frac{3(6k-2)-2(6k-5)}{2(6k-2)-(6k-5)}=\frac{6k+4}{6k+1}$.

Hence $r_k-1=\frac{3}{6k-5}$ and
$$\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{9}{(6k-5)(6k+1)}=\frac96\sum_{k\ge1}\Big(\frac1{6k-5}-\frac1{6k+1}\Big)=\frac32\cdot1=\frac32.$$

**Answer: $\frac32$**

chmmc-cmm-2023-team-04.title: Characterise sus pairs
chmmc-cmm-2023-team-04.body:
Work on an $n\times n$ grid ($n=11$) with vents $v_0$ (top left) and $v_1$ (bottom right). Let $d$ be taxicab distance. A pair $(a,b)$ is sus iff teleporting is strictly faster than walking: $d(a,v_0)+\tfrac12+d(v_1,b)<d(a,b)$ or $d(a,v_1)+\tfrac12+d(v_0,b)<d(a,b)$. All distances are integers, so "$<$ with the $\frac12$" means $d(a,v_0)+d(v_1,b)\le d(a,b)-1$.

Put $a=(x_0,y_0)$, $b=(x_1,y_1)$ and let $\tilde d(a,b)=|(y_1-x_1)-(y_0-x_0)|\le d(a,b)$ (distance between the diagonals through $a$ and $b$). Translating the grid so that $v_1$ lands on $v_0$ shows that the teleport condition is equivalent to $\tilde d(a,b)\ge n$. (If $d(a,b)\le n-1$ then $\tilde d\le n-1$ and walking is never beaten.) So for each $a$, the sus partners $b$ form $B(a)=\{b:\tilde d(a,b)\ge n\}$.

For $1\le d\le n-1$ there are $2d$ squares $a$ at distance $d-1$ from a vent ($d$ near each vent), and for each of them $B(a)$ is a right triangle with legs $n-d$, i.e. $\frac{(n-d)(n-d+1)}2$ squares. Squares on the main diagonal give no sus partners. Therefore
$$\#=\sum_{d=1}^{n-1}d\,(n-d)(n-d+1).$$
Replacing $d$ by $n-d$ leaves the sum unchanged, so averaging gives $\frac{n+2}{2}\sum d(n-d)=\frac{n+2}2\cdot\frac{n(n-1)(n+1)}6=\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)(n-1)}{12}$. For $n=11$: $\frac{11\cdot12\cdot13\cdot10}{12}=1430$.

**Answer: 1430**

chmmc-cmm-2023-team-04.title: Brute-force check
chmmc-cmm-2023-team-04.body:
Enumerating all $121^2$ ordered pairs and comparing $\min$(walking distance, via-vent distance) with the walking distance, the number of pairs where the vent route is strictly shorter is $1430$.

**Answer: 1430**

chmmc-cmm-2023-team-05.title: Power of a point
chmmc-cmm-2023-team-05.body:
Let $B'$ be the reflection of $B$ over $AC$. Since $\angle A+\angle B+\angle C=180^\circ$,
$$\angle HBD=\tfrac32A+\tfrac12B-\tfrac12C=A+90^\circ-C .$$
The triangle is acute ($8^2<6^2+7^2$), so $H$ is inside it, and $H$ lies on segment $BB'$ because $BH\perp AC$. Also $\angle HAB'=\angle HAC+\angle CAB'=(90^\circ-C)+A$, which equals $\angle HBD=\angle B'BD$. Thus $A$ and $B$ see the segment $B'D$ under the same angle, so $B',A,B,D$ are concyclic, and $D$ lies on ray $AH$ beyond $H$. The chords $AD$ and $BB'$ meet at $H$, so
$$HA\cdot HD=HB\cdot HB'.$$
Let $R$ be the circumradius. Then $HA=2R\cos A$, $HB=2R\cos B$, and $HB'=BB'-BH$ with $BB'=2h_B=\frac{4[ABC]}{AC}$.

Compute $\cos A=\frac{36+64-49}{96}=\frac{17}{32}$, $\cos B=\frac{36+49-64}{84}=\frac14$, $\sin B=\frac{\sqrt{15}}4$, $R=\frac{AC}{2\sin B}=\frac{16\sqrt{15}}{15}$, and $[ABC]=\frac12\cdot6\cdot7\sin B$ so $BB'=\frac{2\cdot 6\cdot 7\sin B}{8}=\frac{21\sqrt{15}}{8}$.

$$HD=\frac{HB\cdot HB'}{HA}=\frac{\cos B}{\cos A}\Big(BB'-2R\cos B\Big)=\frac{1/4}{17/32}\Big(\frac{21\sqrt{15}}8-\frac{8\sqrt{15}}{15}\Big)=\frac{8}{17}\cdot\frac{251\sqrt{15}}{120}=\frac{251\sqrt{15}}{255}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{251\sqrt{15}}{255}$**

chmmc-cmm-2023-team-05.title: Numerical check
chmmc-cmm-2023-team-05.body:
Place $B=(0,0)$, $C=(7,0)$, find $A$ and $H$, then search along line $AH$ for the point $D\ne H$ with $\angle HBD$ equal to the required value. The search returns $DH\approx3.8122$, and $\frac{251\sqrt{15}}{255}\approx3.8122$.

**Answer: $\frac{251\sqrt{15}}{255}$**

chmmc-cmm-2023-team-06.title: Encode as a bit array
chmmc-cmm-2023-team-06.body:
Encode $\mathcal B$ as a $7\times8$ array of bits: entry $(i,j)=1$ iff $j\in B_i$. For a column $j$ let $S_j=\{i:(i,j)=1\}$. Then $\bigcap_{i\in I}B_i\ne\emptyset$ iff $I\subseteq S_j$ for some column $j$.

The tuple is good iff exactly one $4$-subset $I$ is contained in some $S_j$. A column with $|S_j|\ge5$ contains at least $5$ different $4$-subsets, so it is not allowed. Hence every column has $|S_j|\le4$, all columns with $|S_j|=4$ must equal the same set $I$, and at least one column equals $I$.

Fix $I$ ($\binom74=35$ choices). Let $J\ne\emptyset$ be the set of columns equal to $I$; each of the other $8-|J|$ columns has $|S_j|\le3$, which gives $\binom70+\binom71+\binom72+\binom73=64$ choices per column. So the count for fixed $I$ is
$$\sum_{k=1}^8\binom8k64^{8-k}=(1+64)^8-64^8=65^8-64^8.$$
Hence $N=35\,(65^8-64^8)$. Modulo $67$: $65\equiv-2$, $64\equiv-3$, so $65^8-64^8\equiv256-6561=-6305\equiv-6305+94\cdot67=-7\equiv60$ and $35\cdot60=2100=31\cdot67+23$. So $N\equiv23$.

**Answer: 23**

chmmc-cmm-2023-team-07.title: Closed form for $f$
chmmc-cmm-2023-team-07.body:
**Lemma.** $f(a,b)=a+b-\gcd(a,b)$ for $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$, and $f(0,0)=0$.

Proof by strong induction on $\max\{a,b\}$. By symmetry let $a\ge b$. If $b=0$: $f(a,0)=0=a+0-\gcd(a,0)$. If $a=b$: $f(a,a)=f(0,a)+a=f(a,0)+a=a=2a-\gcd(a,a)$. If $1\le b<a$: $f(a,b)=f(a-b,b)+b$, and by induction $f(a-b,b)=(a-b)+b-\gcd(a-b,b)$, giving $a+b-\gcd(a,b)$. $\square$

Since $f(2^i,0)=0$, sum over $j=1,\dots,2^i-1$. Then $\sum_j(2^i+j)=2^i(2^i-1)+\frac{2^i(2^i-1)}2=\frac32(2^{2i}-2^i)$. For the gcd: $2^{i-1-n}$ values of $j$ have $\gcd(2^i,j)=2^n$ ($0\le n<i$), so $\sum_j\gcd(2^i,j)=\sum_{n=0}^{i-1}2^n2^{i-1-n}=i2^{i-1}$. Hence
$$\sum_{j=0}^{2^i-1}f(2^i,j)=\frac32\left(2^{2i}-2^i\right)-i\,2^{i-1}.$$
Summing over $i=0,\dots,N$ and using $\sum_{i=0}^{N}i2^{i-1}=(N-1)2^N+1$ gives $2^{2N+1}-(N+2)2^N$. For $N=30$: $2^{61}-32\cdot2^{30}=2^{61}-2^{35}$.

**Answer: $2^{61}-2^{35}$**

chmmc-cmm-2023-team-08.title: Tangent substitution
chmmc-cmm-2023-team-08.body:
By Vieta, $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\frac1{a_3}$, $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=\frac{a_1}{a_3}$, $\alpha\beta\gamma=\frac7{a_3}$, hence $7(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=\alpha\beta\gamma$.

Write $\alpha=\sqrt7\tan A$, $\beta=\sqrt7\tan B$, $\gamma=\sqrt7\tan C$ with $A,B,C\in(0,\frac\pi2)$. Then $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\alpha\beta\gamma/7$ says $\tan A+\tan B+\tan C=\tan A\tan B\tan C$, so $A+B+C=\pi$ and $A,B,C$ are the angles of an acute triangle.

Since $\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{\alpha^2+7}}=\sin A$, the hypothesis reads $15\sin A=12\sin B=10\sin C$, i.e. $\sin A:\sin B:\sin C=4:5:6$. So the triangle has sides $4,5,6$ opposite $A,B,C$: $\cos A=\frac34$, $\cos B=\frac9{16}$, $\cos C=\frac18$, giving $\tan A=\frac{\sqrt7}3$, $\tan B=\frac{5\sqrt7}9$, $\tan C=3\sqrt7$.

So $\alpha=\frac73$, $\beta=\frac{35}9$, $\gamma=21$ and $\frac1{a_3}=\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\frac{245}9$. Next,
$$\tan A\tan B+\tan B\tan C+\tan C\tan A=\frac{35}{27}+\frac{315}{27}+\frac{189}{27}=\frac{539}{27},$$
so $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=7\cdot\frac{539}{27}=\frac{3773}{27}$ and
$$a_1=\frac{\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha}{\alpha+\beta+\gamma}=\frac{3773/27}{245/9}=\frac{3773}{735}=\frac{77}{15}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{77}{15}$**

chmmc-cmm-2023-team-08.title: Verify the roots
chmmc-cmm-2023-team-08.body:
With $\alpha=\frac73$, $\beta=\frac{35}9$, $\gamma=21$: $\frac{225\alpha^2}{\alpha^2+7}=\frac{225\cdot49/9}{112/9}=\frac{1575}{16}$, $\frac{144\beta^2}{\beta^2+7}=\frac{144\cdot1225}{1792}=\frac{1575}{16}$, $\frac{100\gamma^2}{\gamma^2+7}=\frac{44100}{448}=\frac{1575}{16}$. All three agree, and $7(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=\frac{1715}{9}=\alpha\beta\gamma$, so these are the roots of $a_3x^3-x^2+a_1x-7$ with $a_3=\frac9{245}$ and $a_1=\frac{77}{15}$.

**Answer: $\frac{77}{15}$**

chmmc-cmm-2023-team-09.title: Apollonius circle
chmmc-cmm-2023-team-09.body:
Let $AD,BD,CD$ meet the circumcircle of $ABC$ again at $A_1,B_1,C_1$. The angle condition becomes $\angle B_1CC_1=\angle A_1AB_1$ (inscribed angles), so $A_1B_1=B_1C_1$. Similar triangles ($\triangle ABD\sim\triangle B_1A_1D$, etc.) then give
$$\frac{AB}{BC}=\frac{C_1A}{CA_1}=\frac{AD}{DC},$$
so $D$ lies on the Apollonius circle $\Gamma_B$ of $A,C$ with ratio $AB:BC=2:3$. The feet $K_1,K_2$ of the internal and external bisectors of $\angle ABC$ on $AC$ lie on $\Gamma_B$ and $K_1K_2$ is a diameter.

With $AC=20$: $AK_1=8$, $AK_2=40$ (external, beyond $A$). Since $AE=7$: $EK_1=1$, $EK_2=47$. By Stewart's theorem in $\triangle ABC$ with cevian $BE$: $BE^2\cdot20+7\cdot13\cdot20=10^2\cdot13+15^2\cdot7$, so $BE=\frac{\sqrt{211}}2$.

Power of $E$ with respect to $\Gamma_B$: $BE\cdot ED=EK_1\cdot EK_2=47$, so $ED=\frac{94}{\sqrt{211}}$ and
$$BD=\frac{\sqrt{211}}2+\frac{94}{\sqrt{211}}=\frac{211+188}{2\sqrt{211}}=\frac{399\sqrt{211}}{422}.$$
(The other solution of the angle condition is the cyclic quadrilateral, excluded by hypothesis.)

**Answer: $\frac{399\sqrt{211}}{422}$**

chmmc-cmm-2023-team-09.title: Numerical check
chmmc-cmm-2023-team-09.body:
Place $A=(0,0)$, $C=(20,0)$, $E=(7,0)$, find $B$, and slide $D$ along ray $BE$ beyond $E$. The angle condition holds for exactly two positions: $BD\approx19.79$ (cyclic, $BE\cdot ED=AE\cdot EC=91$) and $BD\approx13.734$. The non-cyclic one is $13.734=\frac{399\sqrt{211}}{422}$.

**Answer: $\frac{399\sqrt{211}}{422}$**

chmmc-cmm-2023-team-10.title: Quadratic Gauss sum
chmmc-cmm-2023-team-10.body:
Let $p=167\equiv7\pmod8$ and $z=\sum_{0\le a<p}\xi^{a^2}$.

1. $|z|=\sqrt p$: $z\bar z=\sum_{a,b}\xi^{(a-b)(a+b)}=\sum_{r,s}\xi^{rs}=p$ (the substitution $r=a-b$, $s=a+b$ is a bijection mod $p$; the sum over $s$ vanishes unless $r=0$).
2. $z=\pm i\sqrt p$: since $p\equiv3\pmod4$, exactly one of $t,-t$ is a nonzero square, so $z+\bar z=2+2\sum_{u\ne0}\xi^u=0$, and $z$ is purely imaginary.
3. $\sum_{a}\xi^{2a^2}=z$, because $2$ is a quadratic residue mod $167$ ($13^2\equiv2$), so multiplication by $2$ permutes the nonzero squares, and $\sum_a\xi^{2a^2}$ is a rearrangement of $z$.

Now $z^2=\sum_a\xi^{2a^2}+2\sum_{0\le a<b<p}\xi^{a^2+b^2}$, so $\sum_{0\le a<b<p}\xi^{a^2+b^2}=\frac{z^2-z}2$. Removing the terms with $a=0$ (they sum to $z-1$):
$$S=\sum_{0<a<b<p}\xi^{a^2+b^2}=\frac{z^2-z}{2}-(z-1)=\frac{z^2-3z+2}2=\frac{-p+2-3z}{2}.$$
With $z=\pm i\sqrt p$: $|S|^2=\Big(\frac{p-2}2\Big)^2+\frac{9p}4=\frac{(p-2)^2+9p}{4}=\frac{(p+1)(p+4)}{4}$. For $p=167$: $|S|=\frac{\sqrt{168\cdot171}}2=\frac{\sqrt{28728}}2=\frac{6\sqrt{798}}2=3\sqrt{798}$.

**Answer: $3\sqrt{798}$**

chmmc-cmm-2023-team-10.title: Numerical check
chmmc-cmm-2023-team-10.body:
Summing $\xi^{a^2+b^2}$ over all $0<a<b<167$ with $\xi=e^{2\pi i/167}$ numerically gives $-82.5-19.38i$, whose modulus is $84.747\ldots=3\sqrt{798}$.

**Answer: $3\sqrt{798}$**
